name: Hana Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to your employer or anyone selling AI, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Hana Tanaka, 43, and I’ve got my vocational certificate but I’m still the junior person on a line crew. We meet at the electricity company yard before sunrise, check the truck and the isolation sheet, then head to whichever pole or cable is causing trouble. I like being outside and seeing lights come back on. I hate how a late callout lands exactly when my two children need collecting from school; my partner Nia usually handles that while I’m on the road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part are you still learning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Reading a damaged crossarm from the ground is harder than it looks, and I ask the senior worker before I choose a rigging point. My pay is high for this job because of shift premiums, and we have more than six months of expenses saved, though the mortgage payment is real. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy my training notes, but I don’t trust it to tell me a line is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the yard I’d say the new software can finish a form, but the crew still has to isolate the feeder and climb. I’m happy if a dull report takes ten minutes less. My gloves will still need drying on the radiator after a wet shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I’d be relieved to get more supervised time on actual repairs. I’m still slower than the others, and a supervisor may notice that before any machine does. Our savings are sound, but the school holidays and mortgage make me watch the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking the early callouts and ask Marta, the senior worker, to check my rigging choices each Friday. In the first year I’d use the saved paperwork time for pole inspections, not buy anything new. I’d keep our monthly mortgage transfer exactly where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the technology, though I still feel the little sting of being new at 43. A normal wet Monday would worry me more than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when you get another repair you have not seen before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta has corrected me twice about where to put a sling, and I wrote both cases in my pocket notebook. I’d rather ask again in front of the crew than pretend I saw a crack I missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the household budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia and I already look at the mortgage statement on the first Sunday each month. We wouldn’t cancel the children’s swimming lessons just because a report got quicker.

say: I would tell the crew that **forms** may get quicker, while our repair work still needs people on the line.
I would welcome ten minutes back for **inspections** during a crowded shift.
think: I want more **supervised repairs** because I am still learning the safest rigging choices.
Our **savings** cover a long stretch, although school holidays and the mortgage still enter my calculations.
do: Take **early callouts** and ask Marta to review rigging choices each Friday.
Use freed **paperwork time** for pole inspections during the first year.
feel: Calm about the software, with a small **sting** about being junior.
S0.quote: My gloves will still need drying on the radiator after a wet shift.
fieldNote: Hana keeps the **physical repair** at the centre of her account and treats quicker forms as a modest convenience.
Her confidence rests on **savings** and available shifts, while she remains candid about being a beginner in middle age.

steps.text: Take early callouts and inspect poles with the crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that computer schedules might be useful, but nobody should quietly drop a second person from a live-line job. I’d want our union rep at the table before management changes the crew size. A screen can book a truck; it cannot feel a loose fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning office might shrink first, and then they may try to make each field crew cover more ground. I’ve got enough put aside to refuse a dangerous shortcut, but I don’t want my higher shift pay stripped away. There are other electricity companies nearby, which helps me say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d bring the crew-size question to our union meeting and ask for the written safety rule. If software starts routing our jobs, I’d trial it alongside the paper route with Marta. In the first year I’d keep recording travel times so I can show where its schedule fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy is the word. My hands-on job looks present for years, but the clock on our shift could get squeezed. I don’t like being told the route is obvious by something that has never stood in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show that a new route is unsafe or wasteful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down the day a computer sends us across town twice, including the mileage and the time. A complaint needs more than my irritation if it’s going to change the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the change touch your family first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn’t drop our savings to buy a gadget. I would keep the child-care arrangement with Nia and push for an honest crew plan before overtime disappears.

say: I would accept **better scheduling** if the electricity company keeps safe crew sizes.
I would ask our **union rep** to see any staffing change before management applies it.
think: I expect the **planning office** to shrink before our line crew does.
My **shift premiums** could narrow if software packs more jobs into each day.
do: Raise the **crew-size rule** at the next union meeting.
Trial software **routes** beside the paper plan and record wasted journeys.
feel: Uneasy about a **tighter clock** despite a continuing need for repairs.
S1.quote: A screen can book a truck; it cannot feel a loose fitting.
fieldNote: Her public argument concerns **crew safety**, while her private worry focuses on the extra pay attached to long shifts.
She proposes a **route log** that could challenge management with evidence from actual travel rather than instinct alone.

steps.text: Raise safe crew sizes at the next union meeting
Trial the routing software beside Marta and record bad journeys

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell people to stop pretending a clever screen and a climbing robot arrive together. If thinking work goes in 2028, the field crews still have about three years before those robots arrive around 2031. I’d also tell the company not to gamble with isolation rules in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 45 when the thinking system arrives and 48 when those robots turn up. My reports and schedules could vanish first, but I would still have paid line work in that gap. Once a machine can repair lines as well as us, I don’t know how many crews the company keeps; I’m too junior to assume I’m chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a meeting with our union rep about retraining rights and keep a written log of the repairs I can do without prompting. Through 2028 and 2029 I’d continue on the truck, while asking the training office if it funds substation testing. In 2031 I’d apply for that training if it is open, and also apply to nearby electricity companies for remaining crew posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The savings buy time but not another whole career. I can picture the mortgage being paid in 2029; I cannot honestly promise the same wage after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my two children that Mum is still going to work tomorrow, and that adults are learning new work too. They don’t need my worst forecast over breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the training place is unavailable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the training office says no, I’d still send applications to the nearby utilities. I would not withdraw the savings just to sit at home waiting for a perfect role.

say: I would separate the **2028 thinking change** from the robots expected around 2031.
I would ask the company to protect **isolation rules** while decisions are rushed.
think: I expect paid **line work** for the gap, but robot repairs could reduce crews after 2031.
My junior standing makes the **2031 roster** uncertain even with more than six months saved.
do: Meet the **union rep** now about rights to funded training.
Continue **truck shifts** through 2029 and seek funded substation testing before the robots arrive.
Apply to nearby **utilities** for crew openings if our positions shrink in 2031.
feel: Anxious about **income after 2031**, while clear that the savings offer some room to act.
S2.quote: The savings buy time but not another whole career.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 desk impact** from the 2031 arrival of capable repair robots, avoiding an immediate claim of field unemployment.
Her **junior status** shapes a practical search for funded testing skills and applications across several local electricity companies.

steps.text: Meet the union rep about funded training rights
Request funded substation testing training before 2031
Apply to nearby utilities for remaining crew jobs in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us enough notice to hold a proper safety discussion. Thinking systems could take the office jobs by 2031, but robots for field repairs are on the 2034 clock. I’d ask the company to publish what happens to apprentices, because I’m still close to that level myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when the thinking system comes, I should have more time on lines than I do now. At 51, when robots arrive, I may still have years of work ahead, and my wage is not guaranteed. I’d rather choose a new skill while the mortgage balance is falling than wait for a redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I’d ask the training office for its substation testing requirements and speak to the union about paid study time. If a funded place opens, I’d enroll and practise on our scheduled maintenance days. In 2032 I’d keep doing line repairs while I apply for testing vacancies inside the company; by 2034 I’d compare an outside offer if the robot trial cuts shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now, edging toward anxious as 2034 gets closer. There’s time to learn, and our savings mean I needn’t take the first bad offer. The children will be older, but the mortgage will still need paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the training office beyond the course name?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask how many maintenance vacancies exist, not accept a promise that everybody can become a supervisor. A course only helps if the firm has actual posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if field shifts fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia and I would keep paying the mortgage on schedule. If my shifts fell in 2034, we’d pause the expensive summer trip before touching our emergency account.

say: I would ask for a **published plan** for junior workers before office tasks change in 2031.
I would distinguish the **2034 robot date** from the earlier change to planning and records.
think: I may have stronger **line skills** by 2031, yet field income after 2034 remains uncertain.
Our **mortgage** will still exist when the children are older and robots arrive.
do: Ask the training office about **testing vacancies** and funded study time now.
Enroll in **substation testing** if funded, while continuing line repairs through 2032.
Compare an outside **utility offer** if robots reduce shifts in 2034.
feel: Uneasy with time to prepare, but more **worried** as the 2034 field date approaches.
S3.quote: A course only helps if the firm has actual posts.
fieldNote: Hana treats the five-year warning as **working time**, asking for vacancy numbers rather than trusting a broad retraining pledge.
Her proposed summer-trip cut reflects **mortgage discipline**; she does not describe using savings as an immediate response.

steps.text: Enroll in funded substation testing if a place opens
Compare outside utility offers if shifts fall in 2034
Pause the summer trip if field shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade is long enough to make a decent plan rather than panic in the yard. The thinking system arrives in 2036, when I’m 53; the climbing robots come around 2039, when I’m 56. I’d still want a union seat in decisions about any new crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children would be grown by then, not two school pickups on the calendar. I could imagine reducing line shifts near 56, but I cannot count on a pension amount I have not checked. If I stay on the tools without building another option, even a long warning can run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request my actual retirement statement and ask our union about how service years count. Over the coming decade I’d keep taking paid repairs while trying for a funded substation testing place, not quit on a promise. In 2037 I’d review the mortgage balance with Nia and apply for an inspection post if one is vacant; in 2039 I’d decide whether to reduce shifts only after seeing our income figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy rather than scared. I have time and a solid cushion, but 56 is not automatically retirement. I want the choice to be ours, not a surprise in the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What numbers would you check before reducing shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the retirement statement beside the mortgage schedule and see what numbers are real. I’ve watched colleagues talk about retiring early without checking the monthly amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no inspection vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If an inspection post never opens, I’d keep working as long as the crew still needs me and it’s safe. I won’t tell Nia the house is covered on the strength of a guess.

say: I would call for a **union seat** in staffing decisions over the decade.
I would tell colleagues that **2036 thinking AI** and 2039 repair robots are different milestones.
think: By 2039 our children are **grown**, but I cannot presume a pension or a free house.
I could reduce field shifts near **56** only if the real household figures support it.
do: Request a **retirement statement** and check service years with the union now.
Continue paid repairs while seeking **funded testing** before the 2036 change.
Apply for an **inspection post** in 2037 if one exists.
feel: Uneasy about the later field change, yet grateful for **time** to make an informed choice.
S4.quote: I want the choice to be ours, not a surprise in the depot.
fieldNote: Her decade plan starts with **actual account figures**, not an assumed pension or an automatic retirement at 56.
She would continue **paid work** and seek an inspection vacancy while the children become independent and the mortgage declines.

steps.text: Ask the union how service years affect retirement
Keep taking paid line repairs through the transition
Seek a funded substation testing place before 2036
Apply for an inspection vacancy in 2037 if available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I’d still be learning when the company starts making big choices, and the robots follow around 2031. A written promise of paid training with real vacancies would help; so would a union seat before management changes crew numbers. I don’t need a speech about how adaptable workers can be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn’t ask who is accountable when a machine says a line is isolated and somebody climbs. That decision has a person’s body underneath it. My children will understand a changed job someday; they won’t understand a preventable accident.

headlineQuote: My children will understand a changed job someday; they won’t understand a preventable accident.
portrait: Hana is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate, high shift pay, strong savings, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses AI for **training notes**, but depends on senior checks for rigging and demands evidence before changing field practice.
Her **union focus** follows a concern that tighter schedules or smaller crews could make dangerous work less safe.
Across the AGI dates she keeps **paid repairs** in view, seeks funded testing skills and checks real vacancies before trusting a transition.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because major staffing decisions would start while she is still learning, before repair robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid training** linked to real vacancies and a union seat before crew numbers change.
